prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map captures the open outdoor sports field as a continuous ground-plane gradient from bright white at the bottom foreground (1–2 m in front of the camera wearer) to dark grey at the soccer goal (25–35 m ahead), stadium bleachers (40–60 m), and black sky above. It silhouettes the nearer player in dark clothing on the left at roughly 8–15 m away (whose right side is partially cut off by the left frame edge in frame 2 as the camera pans right) and the second player standing in the goal ~25–35 m away and ~15–20 m to the right/behind the first player across frames 2–5. Nothing is within arm's reach (~0.7 m) of the camera wearer or the players, though the foreground ground plane appears brightest in frames 3 and 5 when the camera tilts slightly downward. Compared to the RGB strip alone, the depth map makes the thin goalposts, light poles, and distant goalkeeper stand out more clearly against the cluttered stadium background. However, it is unreliable for small objects on the turf—completely losing the ball ~10 m ahead in frame 1 and blending the white soccer ball ~1.5–2 m ahead at the bottom of frame 3 into the bright ground gradient—and provides no cues for which way either person is facing or looking.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates foreground people and balls on a black background across the 5 frames as the camera wearer pans right across the pitch. It tracks the left-side `person` (~8–15 m away, half-occluded by the left image boundary in frame 2 before appearing further into the left field in frames 3–5), detects the distant `person` inside the goal (~25–35 m ahead and ~15–20 m right of the first player) in frames 2–5, and labels the white `sports ball` on the grass ~1.5–2 m in front of and below the camera wearer in frame 3 (still beyond arm's reach). This map highlights the tiny distant goalkeeper and the foreground ball in frame 3 much more distinctly than the wide-angle RGB image. However, it is unreliable where it misclassifies a small object on the ground near the left goalpost (~28 m away) as an extra `person` in frame 2, misses the ball on the grass near the left player in frame 1, and omits the goal frame, bleachers, and ground plane entirely. It also cannot convey metric distance or whether the players face toward or away from the camera wearer.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand pose map is completely black across all 5 frames, failing to render any yellow body or magenta hand skeletons for the scene. Consequently, it provides nothing beyond the RGB strip and is completely unreliable for detecting the player on the left (~8–15 m away) or the goalkeeper in the centre-right goal (~25–35 m away, ~15–20 m from the first player) due to their small pixel scale in the wide-angle egocentric view. Relying on the RGB context instead shows that no person or object is within arm's reach of the camera wearer (the closest object is the white ball ~1.5–2 m ahead on the ground in frame 3) or of the two players. The RGB strip also shows that as the camera pans right and tilts slightly across frames 1–5, the left player approaches slightly and is partly clipped by the left frame border in frame 2 before retreating to ~12–15 m, turning from facing the camera wearer in frame 1 to facing sideways right in frames 2–3 and angled away toward the goal in frames 4–5, while the distant goalkeeper faces roughly toward the camera wearer.
